kA, nA = H.rob_count("A", "beta_S", "excludes_zero")
kAll, nAll = H.rob_count("all", "beta_S", "excludes_zero")

sec_k = H.SEC.get("multiplicity", {}).get("n_bh_reject")

Political budget cycle research asks whether governments loosen fiscal policy before elections, but the evidence is conditional and its size is disputed. We ask whether scheduled national elections are associated with a lower cyclically adjusted primary balance (CAPB; AMECO series UBLGBP, percentage points of potential GDP) in the EU-27 over 1995--2021 (`{python} H.fact("n_obs")` country-years), and whether this association varies with population ageing. Scheduled elections are treated as predetermined, not exogenous, and all results are associations. The analysis was pre-registered: the plan, estimator and interpretation rule were frozen under the git tag `preregistration-v1` before any outcome was related to an election variable. The confirmatory model is a two-way fixed-effects regression with fractional 12-month pre-election exposure, a within-between split of the old-age dependency ratio, a feasible weighted least squares and AR(1) generalised least squares estimator, and wild-cluster bootstrap-t inference with 27 clusters.

The headline result is `{python} H.evidence_core()`. A full year of pre-election exposure to a scheduled election is associated with a CAPB lower by `{python} H.num(-bS.get("estimate"))` percentage points of potential GDP (95% bootstrap-t interval `{python} H.ival(bS.get("ci_lo"), bS.get("ci_hi"))`; Holm-adjusted p = `{python} H.pval(bS.get("p_holm"))`); the interval is not contained in the pre-registered equivalence band of ±`{python} H.num(H.sesoi(), 1)` pp, so the magnitude is imprecise. `{python} H.evidence_limits()` The between-country estimate is `{python} H.est_ci(gB)` per standard deviation and the within-country estimate `{python} H.est_ci(gW)`. Of ten secondary outcomes, `{python} H.cnt(sec_k, sec_n)` survives Benjamini--Hochberg adjustment (the change in the CAPB, which is arithmetically related to the level and is not independent corroboration), and no spending or revenue component accounts clearly for the CAPB association. The CAPB is a model estimate whose first-outturn revisions are of the same order as the associations sought (mean absolute revision `{python} H.fact("revision")` pp; revision standard deviation about `{python} H.num(H.S4.get("signal", {}).get("sd_revision_over_abs_beta_S"), 1)` times the estimated association; Appendix E). Exploratory moderation analyses (fiscal-rule strength, ageing, debt, accession cohort, euro membership) are too imprecise to detect heterogeneity of a relevant size, and none survives multiplicity adjustment. A separate, non-causal rolling-origin predictive module finds that no model of the next-year change in the CAPB is distinguishable from persistence (RMSE ratios to persistence of `{python} H.num(min(rr), 2)` to `{python} H.num(max(rr), 2)`) and that adding the political and demographic block does not improve prediction.

**Keywords:** political budget cycles; cyclically adjusted primary balance; population ageing; scheduled elections; EU-27; pre-registration; wild-cluster bootstrap.
